title: Integrate Liquity V1 Stability Pool for LUSD Collateral Yield
body:
## Problem
Plain LUSD collateral earns 0% yield. Integrate Stability Pool for ~6.28% APR ([Dune data](https://dune.com/liquity/liquity-v1)) to fund governance token buybacks, without disrupting liquidity.

## Solution
Add `StabilityPoolFacet` via diamond proxy. Auto-deposit LUSD to pool on mint; withdraw principal on redeem. Harvest ETH/LQTY yields during redeems for buybacks/compounding (protocol-owned only). Piggyback ops on user txs for gas efficiency.

## Alternatives Considered
- AAVE (~3.24% yield, more complex).
- Leverage/LPs (higher risk).
- V2 migration (future option for multi-collateral).

## Implementation Spec
### ~~Prerequisites~~
- ~~Audit facet (~$10-20K budget).~~
- ~~Integrate `IStabilityPool.sol` (address: 0x66017D22b0f8556afDd19e1e5b5f1cbD89a6C337).~~
- ~~Add 1inch/Uniswap for swaps.~~
- ~~New storage: `totalPrincipalInPool` (uint256), `protocolTreasury` (address).~~

### Facet Functions
- `depositToPool(uint256 amount)`: Call `provideToSP(amount, address(0))`.
- `withdrawFromPool(uint256 amount)`: Call `withdrawFromSP(amount)`.
- `harvestRewards()`: Claim rewards, swap (e.g., 50% to LUSD for compounding, 50% to governance token for buybacks).

### Flows
- **Mint**: Transfer LUSD → Deposit to pool → Mint uUSD → Update `totalPrincipalInPool += amount`.
- **Redeem**: Burn uUSD → Calc principal → Withdraw/transfer principal → Harvest if rewards > threshold (route to treasury) → Update `totalPrincipalInPool -= amount`.

### Over-Collateralization
Value pool as LUSD equivalent (Chainlink oracles for ETH/LQTY). Redemptions: principal only.

### Monitoring/Automation
- Chainlink/Gelato for optional harvests. It would be nice to sell the ETH/LQTY for LUSD and boost holdings as soon as it is rewarded by the stability pool.
- Dune alerts for APR/supply.

## Testing
- Unit: Deposit/withdraw/harvest (Foundry).
- Integration: Mainnet fork; simulate liquidations.
- Edges: Low liquidity, volatility, mass redeems. Gas: <200K extra per tx.

## Deployment
1. Deploy facet.
2. `diamondCut` via multisig.
3. Verify on Etherscan.
4. Phased: Opt-in for new deposits.

## ~~Risks/Mitigations~~
- ~~Yield variability: Fallback to plain LUSD if APR <3%.~~
- ~~Supply crunch: Auto-withdraw if < $10M.~~
- ~~Security: Audit for reentrancy.~~

title: CI: fix `check_storage_layout` for new contracts
body:
There's the [core-contracts-storage-check](https://github.com/ubiquity/ubiquity-dollar/blob/20799bedf5ee4d40d2863653f7bc2fe68a2ce3fa/.github/workflows/core-contracts-storage-check.yml) workflow which checks that contracts' storage is not messed on contract upgrades.

Check these CI runs which fails with the `No workflow run found with an artifact named...` error:
- https://github.com/ubiquity/ubiquity-dollar/actions/runs/11125075713/job/30912062971?pr=959
- https://github.com/ubiquity/ubiquity-dollar/actions/runs/11145695030/job/30975996318?pr=971

The issue is that when a **new contract** is added the [core-contracts-storage-check](https://github.com/ubiquity/ubiquity-dollar/blob/20799bedf5ee4d40d2863653f7bc2fe68a2ce3fa/.github/workflows/core-contracts-storage-check.yml) starts to fail while the expected behavior for the CI workflow to pass because we don't need to check storage layout for newly added contracts (because storage of the newly added contract hasn't been updated hence storage collision could not occur).

So as a part of this issue we should make sure that:
1. [core-contracts-storage-check](https://github.com/ubiquity/ubiquity-dollar/blob/20799bedf5ee4d40d2863653f7bc2fe68a2ce3fa/.github/workflows/core-contracts-storage-check.yml) is not failing for newly added contracts
2. [diamond-storage-check.yml](https://github.com/ubiquity/ubiquity-dollar/blob/20799bedf5ee4d40d2863653f7bc2fe68a2ce3fa/.github/workflows/diamond-storage-check.yml) is not failing for newly added libraries

P.S. Pls provide a QA in the related PR with these scenarios:
1) No storage updates, CI passing
2) Storage update, no collision, CI passing
3) Storage update, collision, CI failing
4) New contract added, CI passing

title: Adding collateral enabled checks for redemption collections might make users uncapable of redeming their funds.
body:
[MEDIUM] - Adding collateral enabled checks for redemption collections might make users uncapable of redeming their funds.

This PR is intended to fix [the bug described in this Sherlock issue](https://github.com/sherlock-audit/2023-12-ubiquity-judging/issues/29). However, the Sherlock report is actually wrong and the vulnerability described must not be considered as an issue in the first place, so the collateralEnabled check should not be added on collecting redemptions.

Enabling/disabling collaterals allows the protocol to add or remove supported collaterals, not to be used under uncertain situations, such as a hack. In such type of situations, the `isRedeemPaused` check can be enabled to prevent users from redeeming if something wrong is currently  happening.

The problem with adding the `collateralEnabled` check here is that if Ubiquity decides to disable a collateral in the future, some redemptions might be already queued, so users won't be able to withdraw their funds.


Recommendation: Remove the `collateralEnabled` check for collecting redemptions.

_Originally posted by @0xadrii in https://github.com/ubiquity/ubiquity-dollar/pull/894#discussion_r1572571068_

title: Formal verification
body:
We should implement formal verification for [LibUbiquityPool](https://github.com/ubiquity/ubiquity-dollar/blob/a1b11e1b944227144d7cc19ab320220d9fce8b69/packages/contracts/src/dollar/libraries/LibUbiquityPool.sol).

Invariants could be:
- user can not mint more Dollars in USD than provided collateral
- user can not redeem more collateral in USD than provided Dollar tokens

Possible solutions for formal verification:
- https://github.com/a16z/halmos
- https://docs.runtimeverification.com/kontrol

We already had a try with formal verification, you may find related scripts [here](https://github.com/ubiquity/ubiquity-dollar/tree/a1b11e1b944227144d7cc19ab320220d9fce8b69/packages/contracts/scripts/smt-checker).

What should be done:
1. Impelent formal verification for the [LibUbiquityPool](https://github.com/ubiquity/ubiquity-dollar/blob/a1b11e1b944227144d7cc19ab320220d9fce8b69/packages/contracts/src/dollar/libraries/LibUbiquityPool.sol) contract (you may create tests in a separate test file like `UbiquityPoolFacet.formal.t.sol` so we could distinguish unit, fuzz, invariant and formal verification tests)
2. Setup testing CI to run formal verification tests on merge to the `development` branch (keep in mind that github action runnners can run for 6 hours). We don't need to run formal verification tests on eash PR since they're really time consuming.

title: Graph Compounding
body:
I'm focusing on the "breakeven line" idea and its ability to accurately express when a position is compounded (yield is withdrawn, and redeposited.) Instead of graphing it as a ray (a line with one "extended" point) we can instead graph it as a line segment (no extended points) from the position deposit time, to when a position's size is modified. 

If we add to the position size, then the breakeven line should be steeper (more fees should be accrued due to a larger position size.) I made a quick mockup using TradingView to illustrate this idea.

title: Dynamic Data Input
body:
# Dynamic Data Input on TradingView Indicator

The first major engineering challenge in order for this to be useful in realtime decision making is to allow for the script to have the capability to dynamically read position data from external data sources. I did quite a bit of research on this, and it appears that TradingView's PineScript does not currently have this capability. 

Currently the variables must be manually input on the indicator. This can be done by double clicking the indicator on TradingView.

![tv](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/4975670/201572439-f6443b3e-5f1c-4abc-bc15-e8a0be86a129.jpg)

Those variables are manually imported off of the data presented by Revert's UI

https://revert.finance/#/uniswap-position/mainnet/312741

The founder of Revert passed me along this draft documentation of their private API. This was current as of 12 July 2022, as such there may have been some changes introduced since. This will allow you to access the information in JSON format. 

[apidocs.md](https://github.com/ubiquity/uniswap-v3-liquidity-provider-indicator/files/9999366/apidocs.md)

---

# Research

I would encourage you to explore workarounds.

In order to maintain [Dollar token](https://github.com/ubiquity/ubiquity-dollar/blob/0a230f977ad91bbfb01dd28bc1d2ea77faed5237/packages/contracts/src/dollar/core/UbiquityDollarToken.sol) USD peg [LibUbiquityPool](https://github.com/ubiquity/ubiquity-dollar/blob/0a230f977ad91bbfb01dd28bc1d2ea77faed5237/packages/contracts/src/dollar/libraries/LibUbiquityPool.sol) provides the following arbitrage mechanic:
1. If Dollar token USD price >1$ (on a secondary market) then arbitragers are incentivised to 
a) Mint 1 Dollar token for 1 USD of collateral in the [LibUbiquityPool](https://github.com/ubiquity/ubiquity-dollar/blob/0a230f977ad91bbfb01dd28bc1d2ea77faed5237/packages/contracts/src/dollar/libraries/LibUbiquityPool.sol)
b) Sell 1 Dollar token on a secondary market
2. On the contrary, If Dollar token USD price <1$ (on a secondary market) then arbitragers are incentivised to:
a) Buy cheap Dollar token on a secondary market
b) Redeem Dollar token for collateral worth 1 USD in the [LibUbiquityPool](https://github.com/ubiquity/ubiquity-dollar/blob/0a230f977ad91bbfb01dd28bc1d2ea77faed5237/packages/contracts/src/dollar/libraries/LibUbiquityPool.sol)

On early project stage any large swap may affect the Dollar token price greatly and the pool (where the swap occurred) may remain unbalanced for a long time which in turn depegs the Dollar token.

As a part of this issue we should create an arbitrage bot (i.e. `nodejs` app) which could be run on VPS or any suitable PAAS (heroku, cloudflare, etc...) to catch arbitrage opportunities in order to keep the Dollar token USD pegged on early project stage.

What should be done:
1. Create a new `nodejs` app that will catch arbitrage opportunities for the Dollar token
2. Add unit tests for basic functionality
3. Prepare a clear README of how to run the bot

Notes:
- It makes sense to create the arbitrage bot in a separate repository.

title: V1: Backfill and validate historical permit payouts (GitHub + on-chain)
body:
## Goals

- Recover historical permit data from GitHub issues and comments.
- Rebuild permits into the current schema and de-duplicate against the database.
- Validate remaining permits against on-chain activity on Ethereum and Gnosis.
- Produce a final report of matched, withdrawn, and unresolved permits.
- Improve the foundation of the XP system
- have near complete auditability with 1:1 ratio of `issue label totals == stored permit totals`, or at the very least, each task having verified/tracked payouts

***

## Scope

### 1. Scrape and reconstruct permits

- Enumerate all Ubiquity-owned GitHub orgs and repositories.
- For each issue:
    - Filter comments created by the `prod` & `dev` UbiquityOS.
    - Extract any base64-encoded permit URLs from comment bodies.
    - Decode the base64 payloads and rebuild permit objects into the current expected shape.
- Exclude any permits that already exist in the production database.


### 2. Ad-hoc / manual permits

- In addition to bot comments, include comments by:
    - `@0x4007` for manually sent claim URLs when the bot was down or broken (personally happened to me).
    - `@gentlementlegen` where claim URLs may have been copy-pasted manually when things were down/broken (I'm positive I saw it happen for another contributor, if not myself).
- Parse and process these comments for claim URLs using the same pipeline as bot comments.
- Treat these as best-effort coverage to improve audit completeness.


### 3. Permit validity checks

- For all reconstructed permits not already in the DB:
    - Check on-chain whether the permit nonce has been invalidated.
        - Case A: The permit was claimed by the `beneficiary`.
        - Case B: The signer invalidated/withdrew the permit via the `owner` address.
- If claimed:
    - Match the permit directly to an on-chain transaction involving the `beneficiary`.
- If not claimed:
    - Attempt to locate the invalidation transaction from the `owner` address; otherwise classify as “assumed withdrawn”.

***

## On-chain validation (Ethereum + Gnosis)

Both options require mapping `beneficiary` addresses to users in the production DB.

### Common requirement

- Map `beneficiary` → user by:
    - Using the current wallet mapping in the production DB where possible.
    - Where mappings have changed, parse the `username` from the original bot permit comment to resolve historical ownership.


### Option A: CSV-based, thresholded

- Group reconstructed permits by `beneficiary` address and sum total amounts.
- Exclude addresses with a total under a configurable threshold (e.g. 1,000 USD equivalent).
- For remaining addresses:
    - Manually export transaction history CSVs from Etherscan and GnosisScan.
    - Parse CSVs and group transfers that match `permit transfer from` patterns from known funding wallets.
- Accept that low-earning contributors below the threshold may remain unresolved.


### Option B: Programmatic, full coverage

- Build a structure such as `Record<IssueUrl, Array<{ ...Permit, txHash }>>`.
- For each distinct wallet address:
    - Page through full transaction history from RPC / explorer APIs.
    - Attempt to match permit parameters to on-chain call arguments or transfer patterns.
- For permits without an associated transaction hash:
    - Group them by contributor and issue.
    - Enforce that each contributor can only successfully claim once per issue.
    - Write leftover unmatched permits to a file for manual inspection.
- Store matched permits (with tx hash) keyed by issue/repo/org.

***

## Scale / complexity

- Expected scale: thousands of transactions and hundreds of missing permits.
- Non-trivial data volume and debugging effort across:
    - GitHub API scraping and parsing.
    - Base64 decoding and schema normalization.
    - On-chain history queries on two networks.
    - Heuristic matching and manual review for edge cases.

title: Implement Differential Reward Distribution for Reopened Issues
body:
When an issue is reopened and closed again, the reward system should calculate and distribute only the difference between previously granted rewards and new rewards.

**Requirements**:
1. Track Previous Rewards
   - Store transaction history with amounts per beneficiary
   - Record payment mode (direct/permit) used for each distribution

2. Differential Calculation
   - Compare new reward amounts with previously distributed amounts
   - Calculate positive differences only (additional rewards)
   - Skip beneficiaries with no change in rewards

3. Distribution Logic
   - Only process transactions for beneficiaries with positive reward differences
   - Handle cases where original payment failed but issue was reopened

4. Error Handling
   - Validate transaction history before processing
   - Handle missing or incomplete previous distribution data
   - Log detailed comparison between old and new reward amounts

**Technical Considerations**:
- Must not conflict with wallet insolvency fallback (generates permits if wallet can't afford payouts)
- Extend Supabase schema to track complete distribution history
- Implement comparison logic in `payment-module.ts`
- Update GitHub comment format to show differential amounts

**Example Scenario**:
```typescript
// Original distribution
{
  "user1": { total: 100, paid: true },
  "user2": { total: 50, paid: true }
}

// New calculation
{
  "user1": { total: 150, difference: 50 },
  "user2": { total: 50, difference: 0 },
  "user3": { total: 25, difference: 25 }
}
```

**Success Criteria**:
- Only processes payments for positive differences
- Provides clear audit trail of all distributions
- Handles edge cases: failed payments, partial distributions should never happen with the insolvency fallback.
- Handle what happens if we change the mode (direct, permits only) between distributions

title: Save Every Registered Wallet
Nomic Embeddings Model for +10% Accuracy
body:
The vector embedding model that we use is slightly outdated. I did some research to see what has higher accuracy, and I found one with 10% increased accuracy. We should make use of it as well as our old model.

## Leaderboard

Model | Top-5 Retrieval Accuracy (%) | Notes
-- | -- | --
Nomic Embed v1.5 | ~86.2% | Highest overall retrieval accuracy in semantic search benchmarks, especially strong on short & direct queries. Open source and highly accurate.
Voyage-3-large | ~75-77% | Best model from Voyage AI, state-of-the-art in industry, notably outperforms OpenAI text-embedding-3-large by ~9.7%. Strong on domain-specific tasks.

## Tradeoff

> When you submit a GitHub comment that exceeds the token capacity of the embedding model, typically:
> - The model will truncate the input at its token limit (e.g., 8,192 tokens for Nomic or 32,000 tokens for Voyage).
> - This means any text beyond the max token limit is ignored, which can lead to loss of context and reduced embedding quality if important content is cut off.

## Solution

> 2. Similarity Functions
> - Key Point: Embeddings from different models generally cannot be directly compared using the same similarity function (e.g., cosine or dot product) unless their vector spaces are aligned.
> - Each model produces numerical vectors in its own latent space, meaning the scale, direction, and semantic meaning may differ dramatically.
> - Comparing Nomic vectors against Voyage vectors directly will yield misleading results.
>
> What To Do:
> - In practice, keep embeddings from each model in separate indices or collections.
> - For each query or search, use the correct index according to the embedding model used: maintain “Nomic space” and “Voyage space” separately.

## Remarks

GitHub comment limit is 65,536 characters ≈ 16,384 tokens (rough estimate.) This means that especially comments with metadata unlikely will be able to rely on Nomic (8,192 max tokens)

body:
Cool to see it always recommends at least one person but it is very much not relevant. 

Whats the timeline looking like to populate the database by scraping the existing closed issues and their assignees @sshivaditya2019? 

### repo/org/global Context Matching

I think we should optimize our logic. Tasks that may look similar but posted in two different repositories may in reality be quite different. Normally I would prefer to matchmake against those who completed similar tasks within the same repository, but we can "fallback" to org context (try to matchmake against any repository's task in the org) and then a final "fallback" to global context. 

Perhaps the simplest way to calculate this could be to subtract relevance "points"

Example:
```
0% adjustment: Same repository matching percentage 
-25% adjustment: Same organization
-50%: Global
```

Meaning for an identical task posted in three different locations:
```
same repo = 100% match
same org, different repo = 75% match
different org = 50% match
```

Just an idea but open to discussing to make this more accurate and simple to implement. 

### Recent Code Changes Fallback

Another idea to always try and match somebody is to check how much of the codebase was authored by whom. If nobody hits a relevance of greater than 25% we can fallback to assigning whoever wrote most of the code in the repository. Surely we can find the stats somewhere. 

### Future Considerations

Because we want the system to always be assigning the right contributor at the right time in the future, we should consider the output of the `/start` command as well, with all its checks. If UbiquityOS is able to run `/start` on behalf of others this can solve most of the problems I can think of. 

Specifically, imagine the scenario where the same top contributor is always recommended to work on the newly posted tasks. title: Codebase semantic search
body:
For on boarding new developers, or just to synchronize existing developers, we should be generating embeddings of our code base. We can do per file or on the function level, depending on which has better performance.

I asked GPT for the best sorting method on the [embedding leaderboard](https://huggingface.co/spaces/mteb/leaderboard). 

Later it clarified that we should be sorting by "retrieval with instructions" for best results. 

[FollowIR-7B](https://huggingface.co/jhu-clsp/FollowIR-7B) is the highest ranked. 

We should be doing this in two steps:
1. Primarily, we should be generating embeddings of the new files when pull requests are merged.
2. We should have a tool that we can run manually (manual dispatch on GitHub actions ok) to generate all the embeddings. This would be expected to be used if there were pushes directly to the default branch and were not added via pull request

### additional context

> For this use case (codebase question-answering), your focus should be on retrieval tasks. Based on the criteria provided, here’s how I would prioritize the metrics:

> 1. **Retrieval Average (15 datasets)**: This should be your highest priority. The better the retrieval capability of the model, the more relevant code chunks it will retrieve when you ask a question about the codebase.

> 2. **Embedding Dimensions**: A higher embedding dimension may provide more nuanced representations of code and questions, improving retrieval accuracy. However, this needs to be balanced with memory usage and model size.

> 3. **Model Size (Million Parameters)**: Larger models tend to perform better in generating high-quality embeddings, but at the cost of memory and speed. Consider how much memory and computational power you can afford.

> 4. **Max Tokens**: A higher max token limit is useful for code because some functions or files can be quite large. You'll want a model that can handle bigger chunks of code.

> 5. **Classification Average (12 datasets)**: Code-related tasks sometimes involve classification (e.g., determining the type of question or identifying sections of code). A higher classification score can help in such scenarios.

> 6. **STS Average (10 datasets)**: Semantic Textual Similarity (STS) is also important as it measures how well the embeddings capture semantic meaning, which is useful for understanding the context and retrieving the right code section.

> ### Sorting Criteria:
> Sort by **Retrieval Average** first, then consider **Max Tokens** and **Embedding Dimensions** for practical handling of code and performance optimization.

> The other metrics like **Classification**, **Clustering**, and **Reranking** are less critical for your specific use case, but they can help refine the quality if you have a secondary need for such tasks.

title: Include PR context
body:
> Could you can try running `/rewrite` on https://github.com/ubiquity-os-marketplace/command-start-stop/issues/154 please?

> It meets all the criteria for it, and would be great to see it in action. (My concern is that it does not factor in the PR or any code at all, which is a huge amount of missing context as it's unreasonable to expect all technical details to be mentioned in the conversation but their acceptance by reviewers is specification discovery in and of itself)


As a contributor who over the years has often taken on ambiguous specs and saw them through to completion, it has been my experience that, oftentimes a lot of ambiguous specs shift product-design and engineering effort onto contributors and it often goes unrecognized the amount of work that gets put in.

For this plugin to work as best as it can it must also have context of the active PR because, in my experience, a lot of what I implement gets accepted without it being mentioned in the spec/issue convo. It only appears in conversation through review if it needs tweaked or rejected so this means:

- anything off-spec which is undiscussed (an inherent acceptance of that deliverable) is unknown to the llm
- it does not surface reviews or PR comments

Finally, it's unreasonable to expect (I think) contributors who have done the extra product-design and engineering work to list all tech specs of their implementation into the issue, before then calling `/rewrite`. Better UX if the plugin/agent handles this themselves.

title: Enhance Kernel with Generalized Request Handling & Secure External API
body:
#### **Summary**  
Expand the kernel's ingress beyond GitHub webhooks by introducing a secure public API endpoint. This will allow external services to trigger GitHub Actions workflows, effectively turning Actions into a general-purpose backend.  

#### **Key Features**  
- **Public API Endpoint**:  
  - Accepts external requests to execute plugins via the kernel.  
  - Supports dynamic execution of actions, enabling broader integrations.  

- **Authentication & Security**:  
  - Requests must include:  
    - `installation ID` (this allows us to target the correct org)  
    - `repository ID` (optionally, to load a specific repo config)  
  - Partners must provide an **encrypted password** stored in their config.  
    - Uses **X25519 encryption** (same system as EVM private key storage).  
    - Clients pass a password in the request header, which the kernel decrypts.  
  - Rate-limiting to prevent abuse.  

- **Execution Flow**:  
  1. Kernel receives an authenticated request with at least `installation ID` and `password`.  
  2. It decrypts the password and verifies the request.  
  3. Executes the specified plugin and returns the response.  

- **Webhook Replies**:  
  - Requests can include a `response URL` header.  
  - The kernel posts the result from the action plugin to this URL upon completion.  

- **Future Enhancements**:  
  - Investigate **cross-plugin communication** via the kernel relay.  

#### **Next Steps**  
- Define API Contract (Headers, Payload Format)
- Implement Authentication & Decryption Logic
- Extend Kernel Request Handling to Invoke Plugins
- Add Support for Webhook Response Delivery

The SDK would handle calling the Action or run it normally as a Worker and in case you're running it locally it would execute Action handlers locally too. 
Sometimes the reason why we need to call it as an Action is because some libraries are not supported by CF Workers so it'd be also good to have an option to run it as an Action even if you're running it locally.
Current hybrid plugins use `ACTION_REF` to know which Action to call but it'd be great if we could somehow get it automatically but I realize that may be not feasible.

At this point I would also consider merging `createActionsPlugin` and `createPlugin` for seamless experience.

I also realized that maybe we don't need kernel credentials to trigger Action from the Worker but only a fine-grained Github token that would only have access to the repo. Because we don't change the payload but only forward it to the Action, we don't need to generate a new signature and we can keep the original.

body:
The permit generation plugin should also optionally be able to automatically invoke a transfer to the beneficiaries. 

This introduces additional complexities because it must be able to estimate the gas fee of the transaction (given that we must support multiple EVM networks, with varying levels of activity, it is not viable to hard code this.)

In an org/repo config we can have a property related to payments `transfer: true`

It should also allow for the kernel operator (@ubiquity) to take a fee[^1^]. This fee should be configured elsewhere, perhaps in Cloudflare Worker Secrets (partner projects should not be able to change this.) Any fees that we take should be direct transfers of Ubiquity Dollars to `ubq.eth`.

[^1^]: This means we have to start thinking about how to capture value from payments moving around in our system. I think that we need to make a superior developer experience with our SDK and permit requests, so that plugin developers can easily capture value from the transactions their plugins are helping with.

title: Spec: daemon-hotfix self-improvement plugin
body:
## Problem
We want continuous self-improvement across UOS plugins without bloating the kernel. Today, the kernel logs plugin dispatch failures and skips workflow/check events to avoid loops, so a dedicated hotfix plugin cannot react to those failures.

## Goals
- Route actionable failure signals to a dedicated plugin (`daemon-hotfix`) with minimal kernel changes.
- Create/update issues in the appropriate plugin repo with enough context to reproduce.
- Optionally propose fixes (PRs) with tests, while remaining safe by default.
- Keep kernel lean: routing + policy gates only.

## Non-goals
- No fully autonomous merges by default.
- No attempt to modify UOS kernel logic beyond minimal event plumbing.
- No brittle keyword/regex-only tool selection for AI-driven decisions.

## High-level architecture
1. Kernel detects plugin dispatch failures (HTTP worker or GitHub Action dispatch) and emits a synthetic event.
2. `daemon-hotfix` subscribes to that synthetic event.
3. `daemon-hotfix` triages, de-dupes, files issues, and optionally drafts PRs.
4. PRs go through normal CI; auto-merge only if explicitly enabled and risk tier is low.

## Minimal kernel changes (proposed)
1. **Synthetic failure event**
   - Emit `kernel.plugin_error` (or similar) when a plugin dispatch fails.
   - Include enough metadata to find the failing plugin repo and reproduce.

2. **Optional workflow/check allowlist**
   - Today `workflow_*`, `check_*`, `check_run.*`, `check_suite.*` are skipped to prevent loops.
   - Add an allowlist so only `daemon-hotfix` can receive these events if configured.
   - This enables detection of failed workflow runs in plugin repos (e.g., `compute.yml` failures).

3. **Safety guardrails**
   - Rate-limit synthetic events per repo.
   - Suppress events caused by the hotfix plugin itself to prevent loops.

## Failure event payload (draft)
```
{
  "event": "kernel.plugin_error",
  "timestamp": "2025-01-01T00:00:00Z",
  "stateId": "<kernel state id>",
  "source": {
    "kernelRepo": "ubiquity-os/ubiquity-os-kernel",
    "environment": "prod|dev"
  },
  "trigger": {
    "githubEvent": "issue_comment.created",
    "deliveryId": "<github delivery id>",
    "repo": "owner/repo",
    "issueOrPr": 123,
    "actor": "octocat"
  },
  "plugin": {
    "type": "http|workflow",
    "id": "owner/repo:workflow.yml@ref OR https://plugin.url",
    "owner": "owner",
    "repo": "repo",
    "workflowId": "compute.yml",
    "ref": "main",
    "manifest": {
      "name": "...",
      "version": "..."
    }
  },
  "error": {
    "message": "HTTP 502: ...",
    "status": 502,
    "stack": "...",
    "category": "dispatch|http|workflow|timeout|validation",
    "raw": "..." 
  },
  "context": {
    "requestId": "...",
    "pluginInputs": {"redacted": true},
    "responseSnippet": "...",
    "retryCount": 0
  }
}
```

## daemon-hotfix behavior (MVP)
- **Triage & De-dupe**
  - Cluster by `(plugin.id + error.category + error.message hash)` within a time window.
  - Reopen existing issue if the same error recurs.

- **Issue creation**
  - Open a GitHub issue in the plugin repo with:
    - Summary of failure + timestamp + correlation id
    - Link to triggering issue/PR
    - Sanitized error details + repro steps (event replay, if available)
    - Suggested next actions (test/trace)

- **Optional auto-fix (guarded)**
  - If configured and risk tier is low, open a PR with:
    - Minimal patch
    - Regression test or replay fixture
    - Reasoning summary + risk notes
  - Never auto-merge by default.

## Safety, permissions, and loops
- **Permission model options**
  1. Run hotfix workflow *inside the target plugin repo* (simplest for auth).
  2. Central hotfix service that mints installation tokens per repo (more powerful but riskier).

- **Loop prevention**
  - If a failure originates from `daemon-hotfix`, ignore it.
  - If a failure is already under investigation (issue open), update issue instead of spamming.

- **Redaction**
  - Strip secrets/tokens from logs and payloads.
  - Limit stored raw event payloads unless opt-in.

## Configuration (example)
```
plugins:
  ubiquity-os-marketplace/daemon-hotfix:
    with:
      enabled: true
      modes: ["issue", "pr"]
      riskPolicy:
        autoMerge: false
        maxAutofixPerDay: 3
      issueLabels: ["bug", "autofix"]
      notify: ["@team-bot"]
      allowlistRepos: ["ubiquity-os-marketplace/command-codex"]
```

## MVP acceptance criteria
- A 5xx from an HTTP plugin dispatch results in a single issue in that plugin repo.
- A failed workflow run (if allowlisted) results in a single issue in that repo.
- Duplicate failures update the existing issue instead of creating new ones.
- No infinite loops or noisy spam during normal operations.

## Open questions
- Should the kernel emit `kernel.plugin_error` for both HTTP and workflow dispatch failures, or only HTTP?
- Should the hotfix plugin support optional local reproduction with cached webhook payloads?
- Do we want a global dashboard for error rates per plugin?

title: command-plan
body:
I was experimenting with allowing codex to plan sprints (post all the GitHub Issues with correct labels, parent/child issue relationships, and blocking/blocked by relationships) using the below prompt.

It works quite well and I think there is value to build this out as a capability for our manager. 

We can write /plan and it can take the spec and break it down into child issues. 

Although come to think of it, I think we should have another dedicated plugin for estimating time labels, meaning that this prompt should remove any label related operations if we do go with that approach. 


---

## GitHub Issues & Sprints

This project manages work via GitHub issues and sub‑issues. Keep specs concise and avoid redundancy.

### Hard Rules

- Do not create or apply sprint labels. Do not apply pricing labels.
- Do not prefix titles with sprint codes (e.g., `[S1]`). Titles must be plain and descriptive.
- Do not add tasklists to parent issues; sub‑issues in the UI are the source of truth.
- Use real newlines in bodies (never literal `\n`).

### Minimal Spec Format (child issues)

- Title: descriptive (e.g., `Sorting: clickable headers with asc/desc`).
- Labels: apply exactly one time label (e.g., `Time: <2 Hours`) and one priority label (e.g., `Priority: 3 (High)`).
- Body:
  - First paragraph: one or two sentences describing the change.
  - `Acceptance:` section with short bullet criteria.
  - `Files:` section with bullet list of paths (optionally with starting line), e.g., `- src/web/app.ts:1`.

### Sprint Parent Issues

- Keep the body to the sprint spec only. No tasklists. No title prefixes.
- Link children using sub‑issues only (UI shows them automatically).

### Parent↔Child Linking (Sub‑issues)

- Use REST `sub_issues` endpoints (underscore). The child must be referenced by its REST numeric `id`.

List children:

```
gh api /repos/<REPO>/issues/<PARENT_NUMBER>/sub_issues -q .[].number
```

Add child:

```
child_num=16
rest_id=$(gh api /repos/<REPO>/issues/$child_num -q .id)
gh api -X POST -H "Accept: application/vnd.github+json" \
  /repos/<REPO>/issues/<PARENT_NUMBER>/sub_issues \
  -F sub_issue_id=$rest_id
```

Verify parent of a child:

```
gh api /repos/<REPO>/issues/<CHILD_NUMBER> -q .parent_issue_url
```

### Dependencies (optional)

- If needed, use REST `blocked_by` to express dependencies. Avoid tasklists for dependencies.

### Issue Dependencies (blocked_by / blocking)

Preferred: GraphQL API (works reliably on github.com). Use these standalone prompts (copy/paste) — no external files.

- Add “blocked by” using GraphQL `addBlockedBy`:
```
REPO=<OWNER/REPO>; TARGET=<issue number>; BLOCKER=<issue number>
issue_id=$(gh issue view -R "$REPO" $TARGET --json id -q .id)
blocker_id=$(gh issue view -R "$REPO" $BLOCKER --json id -q .id)
gh api graphql -f query="mutation { addBlockedBy(input: { issueId: \"$issue_id\", blockingIssueId: \"$blocker_id\" }) { issue { number title } blockingIssue { number title } } }"
```

- Remove “blocked by” using GraphQL `removeBlockedBy`:
```
REPO=<OWNER/REPO>; TARGET=<issue number>; BLOCKER=<issue number>
issue_id=$(gh issue view -R "$REPO" $TARGET --json id -q .id)
blocker_id=$(gh issue view -R "$REPO" $BLOCKER --json id -q .id)
gh api graphql -f query="mutation { removeBlockedBy(input: { issueId: \"$issue_id\", blockingIssueId: \"$blocker_id\" }) { issue { number title } } }"
```

- Read dependencies via GraphQL:
```
OWNER=<OWNER>; NAME=<REPO_NAME>; N=<issue number>
gh api graphql -f query="query { repository(owner: \"$OWNER\", name: \"$NAME\") { issue(number: $N) { blockedBy(first: 20) { nodes { number title } } blocking(first: 20) { nodes { number title } } } } }"
```

Notes
- REST endpoints for issue dependencies exist in docs, but may return 404 depending on token type/feature rollout. Prefer GraphQL for portability.

### Label Policy

- Do not create custom labels; read existing labels and choose from them.
- Allowed: exactly one time label (`Time: …`) and one priority label (`Priority: …`) per child issue.
- Disallowed: sprint labels, price labels, and ad‑hoc custom labels unless explicitly requested.
- Parents (sprint umbrella issues): do not set any time label to avoid double counting.

### Time Estimate Policy (Aggressive Defaults)

- Docs and small copy: `Time: <15 Minutes` (use LLM-assisted drafting and quick edits).
- Minor UI wiring (single header behavior, simple handler, or small filter): `Time: <1 Hour`.
- Moderate client work (URL state, drill-through, saved views, CSV export): `Time: <2 Hours`.
- Heavier but contained UI work (print stylesheet, lightweight charts, design tokens, a11y/keyboard, simple virtualization): `Time: <4 Hours`.
- Re-evaluate if scope expands; prefer aggressive estimates by default and adjust upward only with justification in the issue body.

title: Deadlines Incentive
body:
After a few calls with prospective pilot partners, it’s clear that teams care about **accurate time estimates** and **incentivizing deadlines**. This command should make deadlines more useful while rewarding contributors fairly.  

---

## **Objective**  
Build the **command-deadline plugin** to:  
1. **Encourage accurate time estimates** by tracking task durations.  
2. **Reward early completion** while ensuring deadlines matter.  

---

## **How It Works**  

### **Setting a Deadline**  
- Use `/deadline [date]` to set a deadline on a GitHub issue.  
- The deadline is tied to UTC by default but can be configured.  
- If a GitHub Project View is linked, the GitHub issue should sync there on the timeline view (if configured).  

### **Rewarding Early Completion**  
By default, finishing a task **on time** earns **100% of the task value**. If completed **faster**, the contributor gets a **speed bonus**. If **late**, they either receive **a reduced payout or are disqualified** (configurable).  

---

## **Deadline Reward Ratio Configuration**  

Instead of always giving **double the task value** for instant completion, we introduce a **configurable coefficient**:  

- **`deadlineRewardRatio`** → Controls how much of the task value is used for speed bonuses.  
- Default is `0.25`, meaning a max bonus of **25% extra** for instant completion.  
- If set to `1.0`, instant completion can **double** the reward.  

For example, on a **$1600** task with `deadlineRewardRatio = 0.25`:  
- **Instant completion** → `$1600 + $400 bonus = $2000`  
- **Halfway to deadline** → `$1600 + $200 bonus = $1800`  
- **On deadline** → `$1600` (no bonus, no penalty)  
- **Past deadline** → Payout gradually decreases unless disqualification is enabled.  

---

## **Final Reward Formula**  

```text
reward = baseTaskValue * max(0, 1 + (deadlineRewardRatio * (1 - (actualCompletionTime / assignedDeadline))) - ((1 - disqualificationEnabled) * (actualCompletionTime / assignedDeadline)))
```

### **How It Works**  
- **If completed early**, the reward increases up to `1 + deadlineRewardRatio` times the base task value.  
- **If completed exactly on time**, the reward is **1× task value**.  
- **If late**:
  - If **disqualification is enabled**, the reward drops to **0** at `assignedDeadline`.  
  - If **disqualification is disabled**, the reward **gradually decreases** until **0 at `2 * assignedDeadline`**.  

---

## **Disqualification (Optional)**  
If enabled, contributors **must** complete the task before the deadline or they receive **nothing**. This can be toggled per project.  

---

### **Mock YAML Configuration File**
Here’s a **sample `config.yml`** with all possible settings and their **default values**:

```yaml
commandDeadline:
  timezone: "UTC"  # Default timezone for deadlines (UTC, PST, etc.)
  deadlineRewardRatio: 0.25  # Max speed bonus (0.25 = 25% extra, 1.0 = 100% extra)
  disqualificationEnabled: true  # Whether missing the deadline results in a 0 reward
  projectView: null  # Link to GitHub Project View if deadlines should sync there
```

### **Configurable Behavior**
- If `deadlineRewardRatio = 0.5`, contributors **can earn up to 50% extra** for early completion.  
- If `disqualificationEnabled = false`, contributors **still get some payout even if late**, but it gradually declines.  
- If `projectView` is set, deadlines will be **synced to the linked GitHub Project View**.  

---

### **Final Summary**
- `/deadline [date]` sets a deadline.  
- **Early = Bonus** (configurable via `deadlineRewardRatio`).  
- **On time = Full payout**.  
- **Late = Configurable penalty (default: disqualification, or gradual payout reduction if disabled)**.  
- **Deadlines can sync to GitHub Project Views** if linked.  

This setup keeps the system **flexible, fair, and easy to configure**.

title: New Task Or Edit Pull Arbiter
body:
### Overview

- During pull requests, we need to have a bias of always moving forward. 
- We always need to make an active decision on whether to include requested changes in the current pull or if we should break them off into new tasks. 
- We should use an LLM to help us decide what to do. 

### Ideal Outcome

We seamlessly can review pulls and then the OS can intelligently create a new issue batching the requested changes and link back. Ideal if it can batch similar tasks aiming for between 1 hour and 1 day within the same GitHub issue (I think this is possible with my experience working with Claude 3.5 Sonnet.)

### Implementation

Developer Referrals
body:
In order to increase the size of our developer community, we should pay who refer developers who contribute. Let's call them DevRels.

The vision is to generate a new permit for the DevRel upon task completion. 
- It is unclear to me exactly how to do default pricing (flat fee, percentage) 
- It can be easy to game and squeeze out extra rewards with a self referral unless the DevRel's cut is zero sum from the developer. If it is zero sum, then a percentage would be safest i.e. 5% or 10%. What is the highest percentage we can go before developers get annoyed? Perhaps we can also set a max cap, like 50 USD per reward in addition to the percentage. For example, if a developer receives a 1000 USD reward, perhaps the DevRel cap can be max 50 USD. 
- I fear the rewards may not be very competitive. We can consider high (non zero sum) rewards in the short term to kick things off, then switch it to zero sum mode later.
- We should also consider a reward for every developer referred (this may be implemented as a separate tool though, because it seems incompatible with the percentage or zero sum system)

### Configuration Requirements

- For version one, lets go only with percentages support. Make sure that the percentage is configurable. 
   - This will keep things simple in case the DevRel earns a tiny reward for leaving a small comment etc.
- Make sure that we can toggle zero sum mode (subtract from developer reward to pay the DevRel.) 

### Implementation Overview

We can do this in a couple of parts:
1. the new referral logs in with GitHub at `work.ubq.fi?ref=[github user id of DevRel]` 
2. we associate in a KV store the key being the DevRel GitHub ID and the value being an array of DevRel values. 
```typescript
type GitHubId = number;
type KV = { [key: GitHubId]: GitHubId[] };
```

This feels a little parasitic if a developer accidentally clicks a DevRel's link at some point in the future, especially if they start losing some of their rewards. I think we need some type of system to "undo" a referral. This doesn't feel like the right solution but I'm unsure what is. 

### Sybils
We can protect against sybils based on the age of a GitHub profile as well as a minimum XP requirement. For example, if the developer XP is low then the rewards are zero sum?

title: Allow Users to Select and Configure Specific Plugin Branches
body:
Currently, the plugin installer GUI assumes users always want to configure and install the version of a plugin found on a single, predefined branch (initially hardcoded to `development`, later updated to the repository's default branch). However, plugins often have different versions, features, or configuration schemas across various branches (e.g., `main`, `development`, feature branches, release tags).

Users need the ability to explicitly select the desired branch for a plugin they are configuring, and the system must ensure that the correct manifest is used for rendering the UI and the correct identifier (Action reference or URL) is saved in the configuration file.

**Desired Behavior / Acceptance Criteria:**

1.  The configuration editor should display a dropdown allowing users to select from the available branches of the plugin's source repository.
2.  When editing an existing plugin configuration, the dropdown should pre-select the branch specified in the saved configuration identifier (`owner/repo@branch` or parsed from URL).
3.  When editing an existing plugin configuration, the editor UI should initially render based on the manifest fetched from the *configured* branch.
4.  When the user selects a different branch from the dropdown, the editor UI should dynamically update by fetching and rendering the manifest from the newly selected branch.
5.  When saving the configuration, the `plugin` identifier stored in the `uses` array must accurately reflect the user's selected branch:
    *   For Action-based plugins: `owner/repo@selectedBranch`
    *   For URL-based plugins: The correctly transformed URL corresponding to the `selectedBranch` (e.g., `https://...-selected-branch-suffix.domain.com`).
6.  UI elements should be consistent with the rest of the application.
7.  Informational/success toast notifications should auto-dismiss.

## Main issues

We will have problems saving different branches because it is technically correct to have two similar plugins pointing to two different branches. Similarly the plugin would not know we want to change the target branch but will instead stack plugins from different branches together.

title: premade configs that are hands-off for partners
body:
## Premade Configurations vs. Default Plugin Manifests

We aim to streamline the experience for pilot partners by providing **premade configurations**. This approach reduces the need for partners to manually configure plugins. In addition, we provide two alternative ways to modify configurations:

1. Utilize [this feature request](https://github.com/ubiquity-os/plugins-wishlist/issues/65).
2. Contact customer support for manual adjustments.

### Default Plugin Behavior

1. When a plugin uses `defaults` that are **not** sourced from a **premade config**, it retrieves its configuration from the plugin's `manifest.json` in its respective repository.
2. These defaults originate from `pluginInputs.ts` and are used across multiple infrastructure components, including:
   - This UI
   - Natural language configuration edits
   - Plugin schema and input validation (kernel-side)
   - Other relevant subsystems

#### Opinionated Defaults

There is a general concern about **opinionated defaults**. Instead of enforcing such defaults, we should **only share premade configs with partners**, eliminating the need for them to define their own configurations.

Reference: [Discussion on opinionated defaults](https://github.com/ubiquity-os-marketplace/command-start-stop/pull/151#discussion_r1991092437)

### Configuration Modes

Currently, there are three configuration modes:

- **Minimal**
- **Full Defaults**
- **Custom**

These modes, up to this point, have not been enforced to be unopinionated. Some configurations are highly opinionated and may not align with the principle of **non-opinionated defaults**.

---

## Proposed Solutions

### 1. Establish a Collection of Premade Configurations
- Define a structured set of **premade configs**.
- Ensure each premade config abstracts its functionality at a high level.
- Reduce the cognitive load on partners.

### 2. YAML-Based Template Structure
To further simplify configuration management, I suggest we use a **YAML template** with the following structure:

```yaml
metadata:
  name: "UbiquityOS Standard Config"
  description: "The fully-enabled and battle-tested configuration which we use across all organizations at Ubiquity."
  version: "1.0"

plugins: ...
```

This template includes:
- **Metadata**: Describes the premade configuration.
- **Plugins**: Lists installed plugins with relevant settings.

This abstraction ensures partners **"don’t have to think about it."**

---

## Handling Plugin Expansion

### Default Non-Expanded Behavior
@gentlementlegen [suggests](https://github.com/ubiquity-os/ubiquity-os-plugin-installer/issues/40#issuecomment-2670919061) that plugins should be installed in a **non-expanded state**. This means:

- **Infra fetches only the non-opinionated defaults** when retrieving the plugin’s manifest.
- **If plugin details are expanded**, infra should fetch its specific config **before** relying on the manifest.

### Supporting Only Premade Configs
If we only allow **premade configs** and restrict editing to **already installed plugins**, then:

- Each `premade` configuration will be expanded by default.
- This ensures we avoid relying on **non-opinionated defaults**, which may not align with intended user experiences.

---

## Conclusion

- **Premade configurations** should be the standard approach.
- A **YAML-based template** simplifies configuration abstraction.
- **Non-expanded installations** should default to non-opinionated configurations.
- **Expanded plugin configurations** should fetch predefined configurations before falling back to defaults.

By enforcing these principles, we create a **streamlined, user-friendly**, and **low-maintenance** approach to plugin configuration management.

title: Octokit helper methods
body:
We are using two GraphQL queries for fetching linked issues and fetching linked PRs so the code gets duplicated in each plugin that needs it. 

I think this is helpful for a couple of reasons:
- No duplication of code
- Less bugs because currently each repo have its own implementation (daemon-pull-reviewer's implementation was typed wrongly causing a bug)
- New contributors can use these helper methods without having to worry about implementation

Octokit supports plugins which essentially add methods to the Octokit object. 
Example usage:
```js
octokit.helpers.getLinkedIssues({
  owner,
  repo,
  prNumber
})
octokit.helpers.getLinkedPullRequests({
  owner,
  repo,
  issueNumber
})
```
